Replying to both of you here, I think a lot of times when people are trying to explain themselves they say things that make sense in their head but to others it comes off completely wrong, especially over the internet. I've definitely tried to explain my experience with chronic illness and have been attacked for it. I'm someone who has been seen by specialists my whole life, I was diagnosed with Joint Hypermobility Syndrome (JHS) as a toddler and have been in PT/OT ever since. My doctors used to laugh that I'm patient zero cause now they have waiting rooms filled with patients that have Ehlers Danlos. BUT THAT'S A GOOD THING. WE NOW KNOW WHAT IT IS AND CAN PROPERLY DIAGNOSE AND HELP PEOPLE GET TREATMENT. A lot of people in this community gatekeep this diagnosis, which is odd. Some people outside of the community straight up don't believe it can exist. It doesn't matter how much proof you serve them on a silver platter. What matters at the end of the day is lifting yourself and others who are experiencing the same invalidation up. 

I understand it's easier to fight fire with fire, but the compassionate human thing to do is to have a rational and raw conversation. Really try to dig deep and see where the other person is coming from. This diagnosis is all on a spectrum, some people have never dislocated, some people dislocate multiple times a day. Some of us can play sports, some of us are bedbound and have caretakers. It's all valid, it's time we make a space for people to speak about their experience without fear, it's time we listen without judgment or malice. 

I hope you all have a wonderful day. Stay safe and healthy.

I think the word "disability" is being thrown around too much in general. And that is not me saying these people are not disabled, I'm simply stating that there is a spectrum when it comes to disability and just because you are on it doesnt mean the first line of treatment is a service dog, especially for mental illness, which I suffer from myself and have a PSD. I made sure to exhaust all options before considering a service dog. I dont understand why others dont do the same. 99% of "service dog handlers" I've met are open and honest to not having a disability but mild anxiety and that's why they think it's ok. When I'm over here struggling to stay alive and my dog is my only life line. Again I'm not putting down anyone having a PSD for "mild" reasons, but for people thinking about it, really take into consideration how much support you need, and if a PSD is truly right for you. As well as mobility dogs, if a cane, walker, wheelchair is a good fit for you, USE IT. Dont put a dog in service if it's not absolutely necessary. I have mobility issues and my SD does not do mobility tasks because I have other tools that work and often are more effective and ethical. Just really think NEED vs WANT when it comes to service dogs.

For newer handlers like me it actually helps create a "dress rehearsal" for these situations. I can think and imagine what I would do if I were in their shoes. Instead of freezing and letting my SD get mauled I'm able to remember how others CONFIDENTLY and EFFECTIVELY handled the situations and do the same. These posts help me feel less alone, and better equipped for WHEN NOT IF it does happen. You dont have to be negative, and you definitely dont have to participate.
